courses.title: Online Security & Fraud Prevention
courses.campaignTitle: The Final Firewall: Pause, Verify, Protect, Report
courses.awarenessBoundary: Public awareness learning; no professional cybersecurity, financial, legal, forensic or incident-response competency is conferred.

missions.title: Find the accounts that matter
missions.purpose: Recognise account dependencies before choosing a first protection priority.
missions.knowledge: Explain why recovery access can affect several other services.
missions.skill: Construct a category-only dependency map and identify a high-consequence node.
missions.desire: Identify what is personally worth protecting and one barrier to starting.
missions.action: Complete and review a small dependency map, real and private or fictional, and choose one justified priority.

blocks.heading: Keep your map private
body: Use service categories only. Do not type account names, addresses, passwords, recovery codes or financial details into this lesson.
A fictional map is an equally valid way to practise. No account or login is needed.

blocks.heading: Notice the moment pressure takes over
body: The source uses Raymond as a composite case, not a verified personal testimony. Its reflection question is: where did fear start driving the next action?
Notice the link between emotional pressure and the next account decision. You do not need to describe a personal incident.

blocks.heading: One account can affect another
body: Recovery access can connect several services. A category that can help reset access to another service has consequences beyond its own contents.
Ask which category could reset another. Choose a priority because of its consequences and dependencies; there is no universal category that must always come first.

blocks.heading: Read a recovery relationship
body: A recovery relationship links the category used to regain access with the category whose access can be reset.
Read the connection in both directions: what could be affected if the recovery route were unavailable, and what protection would address that dependency?

blocks.heading: Build a small category map
body: Use at least three service categories and show at least one dependency. Keep identifiers and secrets out of the map.
Choose a first protection priority and explain privately which consequence or dependency supports it.

blocks.heading: Choose what matters to you
body: What would you most want to protect? Use a familiar category or a fictional one; you do not need to reveal what is in an account.

blocks.heading: Make starting manageable
body: What makes this easy to postpone? Consider a smaller map, a mental map or a fictional version if a real audit feels difficult.

blocks.heading: Make and review the map
body: Draw or mentally arrange the categories, show a dependency and explain the first priority aloud or in private notes.
Review the map once. A promise to make it later does not replace this activity.

blocks.heading: Confirm the activity performed
body: After doing the task, identify whether you used a real private map or a fictional map. Confirm that you made the map and justified one priority; do not upload it.

blocks.heading: Review your decision
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Privately draw or mentally arrange at least three service categories, using real categories or a fictional equivalent.
Show at least one recovery or access dependency without including identifiers or secrets.
Name a first protection priority and explain how the dependency or consequence supports it.
Review the map and choose one improvement. Keep the map and explanation outside CAPAi.
aarPrompts: Was your first priority still right?
What will you simplify next time?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M03-R05: approve account-recovery wording; M03-R11: approve responsibility framing; M03-R12: clarify legitimate requested OTP entry.
Accessible fictional account-map diagram, source Raymond case detail and approved example rationale are not reproduced in the blueprint. Add and approve these assets before enabling their practice.
Approve the non-keyed map rubric. Do not invent a numeric risk score or a universal email-first answer.

missions.title: Interrupt the pressure
missions.purpose: Notice pressure, separate cues from proof and move verification away from the requester’s channel.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish a familiar logo or display name from independently verifiable context.
missions.skill: Identify an observable cue, requested action and independent verification route.
missions.desire: Notice the emotional hook likely to rush your own choice and rehearse a respectful pause.
missions.action: Perform a fictional verification conversation rather than only labelling a message.

blocks.heading: A familiar-looking message arrives
body: Start with the action being requested. A familiar logo or display name is a cue to inspect, not independent proof of who is asking.
Practise on fictional messages only. Do not open sample links or contact a suspicious sender.

blocks.heading: Spot pressure without jumping to certainty
body: Fear, urgency, authority, reward and secrecy can make a request feel difficult to question. These are useful observations, not a complete test of legitimacy.
When information is incomplete, uncertainty is an acceptable conclusion. State the observable reason for pausing and what you need to verify.

blocks.heading: Separate three questions
body: For a parcel, reset, boss or friend request, identify the cue you can observe, the action requested, and a way to check through a contact method you already know.
A verification route supplied inside the same suspicious request remains controlled by that request. Explain how your next channel is independent.

blocks.heading: Inspect two fictional requests
body: Use two fictional practice messages. For each, name the pressure or identity cue and say exactly what the message asks you to do.
Separate what the message demonstrates from what it merely claims. Do not invent missing evidence or accuse a real person.

blocks.heading: Choose the next channel
body: Explain whether you have enough evidence to act. If verification is needed, identify a known independent route and why it is independent.
Review your reasoning and retry any unclear part without a time limit.

blocks.heading: Practise a respectful pause
body: Say or privately write: “I will check through the contact method I already know.”
Adapt the sentence to sound natural while keeping the pause and the independent check. No message is sent.

blocks.heading: Rehearse the conversation
body: Read the fictional request, say your pause, and name a different verification channel. You can play both roles or work with a consenting partner.
Never share a requested sign-in code with a person. A genuine sign-in flow asks you to enter your own requested code into its official sign-in screen.

blocks.heading: Review the cue and channel
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Inspect two approved fictional messages and identify each message’s cue, requested action and known independent verification route.
Rehearse a stop-and-verify interaction aloud, in a private script or with a consenting partner. A solo learner may play both roles.
Do not send messages, click training links, disclose codes or contact scammers.
Revisit one missed cue and choose one verification habit to improve.
aarPrompts: Did you try to verify inside the suspicious message?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M03-R06: approve scenario classification, BNM-related claim and distinct bank rationales; M03-R08: approve verification questions; M03-R12: approve OTP distinction.
Exact canonical message cards and their reviewed feedback are not provided by this blueprint excerpt. Keep practice completion disabled until the cards and their own rationales are supplied.
Do not treat P16’s unspecified message mix or W17–18’s A–E pack as a complete approved keyed bank.

missions.title: Protect access and recovery
missions.purpose: Translate protection principles into a realistic private review without revealing credentials.
missions.knowledge: Explain uniqueness, managed access, MFA or passkeys, and recovery as distinct protections.
missions.skill: Use a checklist to identify an access weakness and an appropriate provider-supported next step.
missions.desire: Resolve a practical barrier such as lockout anxiety, unfamiliar settings or lack of authority.
missions.action: Perform a safe private protection review and one permitted change, or complete an equivalent fictional settings decision.

blocks.heading: Consider protection in layers
body: Length and uniqueness, password management, available sign-in protections and recovery address different parts of account access. Consider them together rather than treating a single setting as a guarantee.
Use the options and guidance offered by the account provider. Recovery needs attention because it can affect the ability to regain access.

blocks.heading: Practise without making a real secret
body: If you practise making a passphrase, make a fictional one that will be discarded. Do not submit it or reuse it for an account.
Actual passwords, recovery codes and credential storage belong outside learning tools and public checking tools.

blocks.heading: Review the account or fictional card
body: Consider whether credentials are unique, which sign-in options the provider supports, and whether recovery arrangements need attention.
Distinguish a weakness you can address safely from a question that requires provider help or permission.

blocks.heading: Choose a supported next step
body: Identify one appropriate improvement and explain why it fits the account’s supported options and your authority to manage it.
If a change could cause lockout or involves controls you do not manage, use the fictional settings exercise instead.

blocks.heading: Notice what you understand
body: Which part of a private review can you attempt confidently? Which part needs guidance? Revisit this judgment after the activity.

blocks.heading: Use a feasible route
body: What would make a private review difficult: unfamiliar settings, worry about losing access, or lack of permission?
The fictional settings route offers equivalent practice. No paid manager or security key is required.

blocks.heading: Perform one safe review
body: On an account you are authorised to manage, review access and recovery privately and make one provider-supported change only if it is safe and understood.
Otherwise review fictional settings and choose a justified improvement. Do not alter employer-managed controls or report a simulation as a real enabled setting.

blocks.heading: Review the protection decision
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Choose an account you are authorised to manage or a supplied fictional settings card.
Review uniqueness, available sign-in protections and recovery without recording secrets in CAPAi.
Make one safe, understood, provider-supported change, or complete the fictional review and select a justified improvement.
Stop if permission or safe access is uncertain. A future plan alone does not complete the activity; use the substantive fictional equivalent.
Privately identify one lesson and one next improvement.
aarPrompts: What safe support route would help next?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M03-R05: security SME must approve password, MFA, passkey and recovery claims and any method hierarchy; M03-R12: approve legitimate OTP distinction.
Supply privacy-safe fictional settings cards and a current provider-neutral checklist with approved scenario rationale before enabling the gate.
The source myth/fact statements are not fully quoted in the blueprint and are not invented here. Self-declaration must not imply verified security effectiveness.

missions.title: Verify the connection and destination
missions.purpose: Separate network identity, encrypted transport, destination trust and the consequence of a task.
missions.knowledge: Explain what HTTPS and a VPN do not establish about a seller or request.
missions.skill: Compare a task and connection context and choose a proportionate verified route.
missions.desire: Give yourself permission to postpone a high-consequence task instead of rushing.
missions.action: Complete a controlled network and destination decision rehearsal with a reasoned next step.

blocks.heading: Consider the airport context
body: The source airport scenario asks you to consider both the connection and the task you want to perform.
Treat this as a fictional decision exercise. Do not connect to an unknown network to recreate it.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Compare the consequence of the task
body: Compare public reading with the source payroll example. What would be the consequence of making the wrong trust decision in each context?
Identify which facts about the connection or destination remain uncertain before proposing a next step.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Encryption is one question
body: Encrypted transport and destination legitimacy are different questions. HTTPS or a VPN does not by itself establish that a seller or request is legitimate.
Ask what a trust signal establishes and what it leaves unresolved. Connection, device, account and human decisions each have a role.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Choose a proportionate route
body: Explain the task’s consequence and what you would verify independently. Consider a trusted alternative or postponing an uncertain high-consequence task.
Do not treat a VPN as proof that the destination is legitimate.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Separate the layers
body: On private paper or mentally, distinguish person, device, account and connection controls. Use the layered-controls worksheet as a decision aid, not a network-configuration task.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Check your reasoning
body: Have you named the task, its consequence, the uncertainty and a trusted next route? Can you explain what your verification does and does not establish?
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Allow a pause
body: What cost would a short pause have compared with an uncertain approval? Think about a feasible next step without urgency or shame.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Rehearse reader, verifier and reporter
body: Using the fictional scenario, play reader, verifier and reporter alone or with a consenting partner. Explain how you would leave the uncertainty.
Do not bypass security warnings, scan networks, download suspicious files or change work-device controls.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

blocks.heading: Review the trust signal
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 27–34 and formative item on slide 60

actionInstructions: Use the fictional airport scenario; do not create a hotspot or a login page.
State the task, its consequence and the uncertainty about connection or destination.
Rehearse the reader, verifier and reporter roles and explain a safe next route. Solo narration is valid.
Optionally review your ordinary auto-connect preference privately under device or provider guidance, without experimenting on unknown networks.
Choose one trust-check habit to repeat.
aarPrompts: Which trust signal fooled your first impression?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M03-R07: approve network, VPN, domain and certificate scope; M03-R06: approve scenario rationale.
Full airport-choice cards, destination illustration and approved domain-reading explanation must be assembled from source and reviewed.
P60 may be formative retrieval under its existing canonical item ID; no duplicate assessment key is included here.

missions.title: Reduce the impersonation script
missions.purpose: Turn a privacy observation into a concrete safer sharing or verification choice.
missions.knowledge: Explain how separate public details can combine into a plausible impersonation.
missions.skill: Identify a disclosure pattern and rehearse an independent check for an unusual request.
missions.desire: Choose a personal boundary that balances connection with privacy without shaming prior posts.
missions.action: Make one appropriate private visibility change or revise an equivalent fictional profile, then rehearse the verification rule.

blocks.heading: Look at the combined picture
body: Separate public details may reveal more when combined than a person intended when sharing each one. Ask what could be inferred from a fictional profile as a whole.
Describe categories of information rather than actual names, routines, locations, recovery answers or private code words.

blocks.heading: A familiar voice makes an urgent request
body: The source executive voice-message case is a composite. Use it to consider an urgent-money request without treating voice recognition as proof of identity.
Explain how a callback or second-approver process could provide an independent check. Do not contact a real person or initiate a payment.

blocks.heading: Choose a sustainable sharing boundary
body: What would you share later, with fewer people, or not at all? Choose a boundary that preserves what you value about connection.
This is a choice for future sharing, not a judgment about past posts.

blocks.heading: Make one proportionate change
body: Identify an observable disclosure, consider who can see it and choose one proportionate change. Use a fictional profile if a real change is unsuitable.
Keep independent verification in place; a publicly knowable challenge question is not sufficient protection.

blocks.heading: Rehearse a second-channel check
body: Speak or privately script an independent check for the fictional urgent-money request. Explain how the contact route differs from the request itself.

blocks.heading: Revise visibility or the fictional profile
body: If authorised, privately adjust one suitable visibility setting or remove an unnecessary public detail. Alternatively make the equivalent revision on fictional cards.
Do not upload posts, screenshots or family data. Keep employer policy and other people’s consent in view.

blocks.heading: Review the inference and boundary
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Inspect a fictional profile or privately review a profile you are authorised to manage.
Identify one disclosure pattern and make one suitable visibility change or equivalent fictional revision.
Rehearse a callback or independent second-channel check for the source urgent-money request.
Keep all profile data, private challenges and code words outside the lesson. Do not make a payment or send a real message.
Choose a sharing boundary you can maintain.
aarPrompts: Was the inference different from what you intended?
What boundary is easiest to maintain?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M03-R08: approve identity, callback and private challenge nuance; M03-R11: review non-blaming tone.
Supply the source-grounded fictional profile/post illustration and full composite scenario with meaningful text alternatives before enabling assessment.
No real posts, location, family data, recovery answers or code words may be collected.

missions.title: Rehearse a calm response
missions.purpose: Distinguish incident categories and practise using an approved reporting reference without amateur investigation.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish financial, crime-report and technical-response routes at awareness level.
missions.skill: Use a current reviewed reference to state an appropriate first contact while preserving official instructions.
missions.desire: Overcome shame and the urge to investigate before asking for help.
missions.action: Perform the fictional bank-alert response rehearsal and identify one improvement.

blocks.heading: Recognise the kind of help needed
body: Financial concerns, crime reporting and technical-response questions can involve different roles. The appropriate route depends on the incident and current official or provider guidance.
This lesson is awareness practice. It does not provide a recovery guarantee or turn a learner into an investigator.

blocks.heading: Keep the exercise fictional
body: No live incident handling, calls, malware forwarding, remote-access experiments or real evidence collection belongs in this exercise.
If you are facing a real incident, leave the exercise and consult current official or provider channels.

blocks.heading: Use a current reference
body: A reporting reference needs clear agency or provider roles and current details. Do not infer contact availability or a reporting deadline from an old training page.
Follow current official instructions. Collecting evidence should not become a reason to delay asking for appropriate help.

blocks.heading: Make asking for help easier
body: What would make reporting difficult? Consider how a supportive person could make it easier to explain what happened without blame.

blocks.heading: Choose the part you can practise
body: Which part of a fictional handoff can you explain now? Which part depends on the reporting reference or official instructions?

blocks.heading: Practise the bank-alert handoff
body: The source exercise uses a fictional account holder, bank or response contact, account protector and support or evidence roles. A solo learner can narrate each role.
Use fictional information and the approved reference. Practise a clear handoff without disclosing secrets or improvising incident-response instructions.

blocks.heading: Keep evidence categories private
body: Discuss fictional evidence categories only. Do not upload incident evidence, sensitive chronology or credentials.
Notice whether evidence gathering distracts from appropriate reporting or crosses into self-investigation.

blocks.heading: Review the first contact and handoff
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: This Action is a fictional rehearsal and becomes available only with the reviewed reporting reference.
Using the source bank-link scenario, narrate or roleplay the account holder, response contact, account protector and support roles.
Use the approved sequence and fictional information only. Do not place a call, forward malware, collect real evidence or test remote access.
Privately identify one improvement to first contact or handoff. Optionally locate an official contact privately afterward without submitting it.
aarPrompts: What would you change in the next rehearsal?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
COMPLETION BLOCKED: M03-R01–R03 must resolve current reporting roles, contact details, conflicting hours and timeline or report-deadline claims.
M03-R04: unify RACE wording; M03-R09: approve evidence and containment scope; M03-R10: approve checking-service limitations.
No hotline numbers, opening hours, deadlines or procedural response sequence are asserted in this asset. The source conflict remains unresolved.
Supply a dated approved help map, exact bank-alert scenario and unified approved response rubric before enabling rehearsal or deterministic checks. Withhold unchanged W47/W61.

missions.title: Make verification a shared habit
missions.purpose: Integrate earlier decisions into supportive group behaviour and an honest review of performed Actions.
missions.knowledge: Explain reporter, verifier and responder roles and why a process cannot depend on silence or one unavailable person.
missions.skill: Respond to the supplier-account-change scenario and demonstrate a supportive report-and-check interaction.
missions.desire: Choose a realistic habit and barrier response without making a public pledge of perfection.
missions.action: Rehearse a small reporting and verification process and review a previously performed protection Action.

blocks.heading: Make the roles understandable
body: A shared process distinguishes raising a concern, verifying a request and taking the appropriate response. Make the handoff clear enough that it does not depend on one person being available.
Responsible habits work alongside technical safeguards and organisational responsibilities. People should be able to report without blame.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: An urgent supplier change is requested
body: Use the source fictional supplier-account-change case. Identify who would report the request, who would verify it independently and who would respond within their role.
Do not change real payment details, send messages or make a payment.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Explain the handoff
body: State how the group would acknowledge the concern, use its agreed independent verification route and handle an unavailable verifier.
Keep uncertainty visible. A process should not pressure someone into silence or treat a familiar request as enough proof.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Respond without blame
body: Practise: “Thank you for raising this. Let us use the agreed verification route.”
Adapt the wording while preserving a supportive acknowledgement and a clear next handoff.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Check the small process
body: Can a reporter raise a concern? Is the independent verification route understood? Are the responder and backup arrangements clear?
Use a fictional family, volunteer group or work setting if there is no suitable real group.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Keep a private one-page process
body: Use the source process worksheet or private notes to connect the roles and the handoff. Do not enter real contacts, incidents or financial details in CAPAi.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Rehearse and revisit
body: Perform the process with a fictional group, alone or with a consenting partner. Then revisit one Action already performed in Missions 1–6 and state privately what happened.
A future event plan alone does not replace the rehearsal and review.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Confirm the performed practice
body: After doing the activity, confirm the process rehearsal and the review of one earlier Action. This is an honest self-declaration, not independent proof of security.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Review the shared habit
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

blocks.heading: Keep the awareness boundary clear
body: Completion covers required awareness learning activities and self-declared application. It does not certify practical cybersecurity competence or guarantee prevention.
Choose a feasible habit to repeat and a safe support route for questions beyond this programme.
sourceRefs: M03-P slides 49–71; final bank slides 56–65 and review 66–67

actionInstructions: Use the fictional supplier-account-change case to define reporter, verifier and responder roles and a backup arrangement.
Rehearse a calm acknowledgement and an independent-verification handoff with fictional information, alone or with a consenting partner.
Privately revisit one protection Action you performed earlier and state what actually happened.
Complete the approved final learning checks with feedback and retry once the bank is released; do not treat a future plan alone as Action.
Choose one improvement to the process and one earlier habit to repeat.
aarPrompts: Which earlier Action worked, and what will you repeat?

missions.title: Replace One Assumption
missions.purpose: Reveal an unconfirmed arrangement and create a dated readiness baseline with one usable correction.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish an assumed arrangement from one discussed and agreed.
missions.skill: Ask a specific question, name the action owner and report what remains unknown.
missions.desire: Recognise one relevant dependency without shame about income or household circumstances.
missions.action: Complete a real clarification or an equivalent two-role fictional rehearsal, then update the baseline.

blocks.heading: Find an unconfirmed arrangement
body: Which part of your plan depends on a promise nobody has made? Begin with a private baseline or a fictional household.
Keep real names, contact details and household arrangements outside the lesson. No real emergency simulation is required.

blocks.heading: Distinguish assumed from confirmed
body: An arrangement is confirmed when the relevant person has discussed and agreed to it. Writing a name in a plan does not establish agreement.
For before, during and after planning, keep the concern, intended action, owner and confirmation method clear. Mark what remains unknown.

blocks.heading: Use the source household
body: The source fictional household introduces Amir, Lina, Mak Som and Sara. Use its planning concerns to practise identifying what has and has not been confirmed.
For the concern you select, state the unknown, the action owner and a specific way to seek confirmation.

blocks.heading: Create a dated baseline
body: Use the eight-topic baseline on workbook page 5 privately or with fictional details. Record its date and make unconfirmed arrangements visible.
Use “arranged” only where the relevant person has agreed. Do not grade your household by money spent or equipment owned.

blocks.heading: Notice the dependency
body: Who would need to understand this if you were unavailable? What makes the conversation difficult? Think privately; no answer is sent.

blocks.heading: Rehearse a clarification
body: Ask one specific non-sensitive planning question and practise a reply. Distinguish agreement, refusal and still unknown.
Speak or write both roles yourself if you prefer. Update the baseline to reflect what the reply actually establishes.

blocks.heading: Confirm the baseline changed
body: Confirm only after a clarification or rehearsal was performed and the baseline revised. Scheduling a future conversation alone does not complete this activity.

blocks.heading: Review the assumption
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Privately date a baseline and select one arrangement that is assumed or unresolved.
Ask a willing household member one non-sensitive planning question, or speak or write both sides of a fictional clarification.
Identify the concern, action, owner and confirmation method. Record agreement, refusal or uncertainty honestly.
Revise the private or fictional baseline based on what was established, then choose one improvement.
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S09: approve privacy and minimum-information boundaries; M04-S13: approve BM safety copy before translation publication.
Supply the source eight-topic baseline and complete P6 household details with accessible text or alt text. The blueprint names the household but does not reproduce all scenario facts.
Instructional editor must approve the concern/action/owner/confirmation self-review criteria and inclusive wording.

missions.title: Read the Risk, Not the Rumour
missions.purpose: Build a three-concern information map with a usable offline backup.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish issuer, issue time, place, validity and advised action, and explain source limits.
missions.skill: Compare the three supplied messages without converting unknowns into facts.
missions.desire: Choose a pause before forwarding alarming material without delaying protection from apparent danger.
missions.action: Perform an information check or equivalent supplied-message exercise and prepare its offline backup.

blocks.heading: Know what an update establishes
body: An update is useful when you know what it establishes and what it does not. Turn three concerns into questions that a suitable source could answer.
Verification is not a reason to expose yourself to danger or delay protective action.

blocks.heading: Ask five information questions
body: Who issued the information? When was it issued? Which place does it concern? What is its validity or scope? What action does it advise?
Keep the time you checked separate from the time the information was issued. A source has limits; information is not a certification that a route is safe.

blocks.heading: Compare three fictional messages
body: The source exercise compares an advisory with limited scope, an old video and an incomplete observation. Treat all source example dates and messages as fictional.
For each message, ask what is established and what remains unknown. Do not turn an old image into current evidence.

blocks.heading: Preserve the source limits
body: An advisory applies within its stated scope. An old video is not proof of current conditions. An incomplete observation needs safe clarification rather than added assumptions.
Choose the next information question without returning to danger for photos or inspecting a route yourself.

blocks.heading: Plan for unavailable data
body: When your usual group or mobile data is unavailable, what makes verification difficult? Choose an accessible written or offline backup you can locate.

blocks.heading: Check a source and find the backup
body: From a safe ordinary setting, check a reviewed official source and privately note the information type and check time. Rehearse locating your written backup without this lesson.
Alternatively use the three source messages, build a fictional concern/source/question map and retrieve an offline fictional backup instruction.

blocks.heading: Confirm check and retrieval
body: Confirm after performing one information check and one backup retrieval rehearsal. Distinguish the source’s statements from remaining unknowns.

blocks.heading: Review the information gap
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Create three concern/source/question pairs privately, using your own ordinary setting or the supplied fictional messages.
From safety, check one reviewed official source and note what it supplies and when checked; alternatively compare all three fictional messages.
Keep issuer, issue time, place, validity and advised action distinct. Do not present changing live conditions as a fixed quiz answer.
Prepare an accessible offline backup and practise finding it without the lesson. Do not inspect hazards or routes.
Identify the unanswered question that will make the next check clearer.
aarPrompts: What will make your next check clearer?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S01: verify official endpoints, scopes and check dates; M04-S07: approve no-exposure and current-hazard caveats; M04-S13: approve BM safety wording.
Exact W8/P17–18 A/B/C message cards and approved feedback must be supplied before deterministic checks are enabled.
No live source links or current availability claims are invented. Any official reference displayed needs tested descriptive links and actual last-checked metadata.

missions.title: Make Preparation Usable
missions.purpose: Produce a realistic preparation checklist and test one usable improvement.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish carry, keep and confirm, and understand the limited three-day planning exercise.
missions.skill: Choose and explain suitable items or arrangements for one source household profile.
missions.desire: Remove the need-to-buy-everything barrier and value accessible, no-cost preparation.
missions.action: Organise an existing safe everyday item or enact the equivalent fictional preparation task.

blocks.heading: Begin with what you already have
body: Can the intended person find and use the item or information? Start with a practical improvement that does not require spending money.

blocks.heading: Separate carry, keep and confirm
body: Distinguish something portable, something kept at home and an arrangement that must be confirmed with another person. Supplies do not replace agreements.
The source three-day exercise is a planning starting point, not a universal guarantee, maximum or reason to delay movement. Adaptation may need suitable advice.

blocks.heading: Do not improvise technical solutions
body: Medicine, powered equipment and generator questions need appropriate provider or qualified guidance. This activity does not teach storage changes, device modifications or electrical work.
Do not handle electrical faults, change medicine use or experiment with generators. No purchase is required.

blocks.heading: Choose a source household profile
body: Use a fictional person living alone, family with an infant, older couple or household needing access support.
Consider whether an item or arrangement is usable for that profile without requesting real diagnoses or equipment details.

blocks.heading: Sort and explain a choice
body: Sort proposed items and agreements into carry, keep and confirm. Explain how one choice fits the fictional household.
Several safe, reasoned choices may be suitable. Mark provider-dependent questions as advice needed instead of inventing a solution.

blocks.heading: Find a no-cost improvement
body: What can be organised without spending? Which gap needs advice rather than improvisation? Choose a smaller feasible task or the fictional route.

blocks.heading: Test whether preparation is usable
body: Safely locate an existing non-hazardous everyday item or written information copy and agree or label a usable storage location.
Alternatively build a fictional paper checklist, demonstrate locating an item or arrangement, revise an inaccessible choice and mark advice-needed gaps.

blocks.heading: Confirm a tested improvement
body: Confirm after the organisation task or fictional equivalent is performed. A promise to purchase something later does not complete Action.

blocks.heading: Review usability
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Choose one source household profile and sort its proposed supplies or arrangements into carry, keep and confirm.
Privately locate one safe existing everyday item or written information copy and establish a usable location, or build the fictional paper checklist.
Demonstrate finding the item or arrangement. Revise one choice that is inaccessible or unclear.
Leave medication, powered-equipment and generator questions for appropriate guidance. Do not experiment or delay protective action.
Update one priority and consider what remains unsuitable.
aarPrompts: What became easier to find or understand?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S02: approve the bounded three-day exercise; M04-S03: clinical/technical review of provider-dependent needs; M04-S04: review generator source guidance; M04-S13: BM review.

Exact source safety warning cards, profile details and sorting rationale need approval before mission activation. No technical quantities, generator placement rules or equipment standards are supplied here.
Provide an accessible sorting alternative; do not require drag-and-drop or a purchase.

missions.title: Make the Plan Understandable
missions.purpose: Combine earlier outputs into a shared plan and revise it after testing another person’s understanding.
missions.knowledge: Describe contacts, support, conditional destinations, owners and review fields.
missions.skill: Explain a plan and identify missing consent, availability or backup.
missions.desire: Recognise that writing somebody’s name does not secure their agreement.
missions.action: Perform teach-back or solo role reversal and revise a specific ambiguity.

blocks.heading: Test understanding
body: A plan is shared when another person can explain it. Use a fictional or redacted copy to test whether the meaning is clear.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Connect the plan fields
body: A usable plan links contacts, support needs, conditional destinations or movement options, action owners and review arrangements.
Distinguish primary, backup and out-of-area contacts. Availability, consent and current conditions matter; a written route is not a guarantee of safe movement.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Identify an open agreement
body: The source Mak Som/helper arrangement and no-reply scenario raise questions about agreed support and what silence establishes.
Which agreements remain open? No reply should remain an unknown rather than being treated as confirmation of safety.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Make the unknowns visible
body: Use workbook page 16 privately or with fictional details. Add an owner and review date for unresolved arrangements.
The real contact sheet on page 17 stays offline. Share a redacted or fictional copy for this exercise.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Consider consent and backup
body: Whose agreement does the plan require? What happens if you are unavailable? An agreed helper or backup may still need a current-condition check.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Try a teach-back
body: Ask a consenting person to explain the non-sensitive plan in their own words. A solo learner can put it aside and then read it as another person.
Find a part that takes a long explanation, answer the source review questions and revise one ambiguity.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Confirm the test and revision
body: Confirm only after the plan was tested and an unclear part revised. Real unresolved agreements may remain openly marked; they must not be invented.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

blocks.heading: Review what the reader understood
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

actionInstructions: Prepare a private plan or fictional/redacted equivalent with contacts, support, conditional options, owners and review fields.
Ask a consenting person to explain the non-sensitive plan, or perform solo planner/reader role reversal.
Check whether a helper and backup are agreed or explicitly unresolved and whether changing conditions could change the plan.
Revise one ambiguity. Keep real contacts offline; do not walk a route, trigger alarms, interrupt power, lift or carry someone, or make real calls for the exercise.
Choose the revision that most improved understanding.
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S05: approve conditional routes, destinations and inclusive support; M04-S08: approve status/role wording; M04-S09: privacy review; M04-S13: BM safety review.
Supply source plan fields, exact Mak Som/no-reply facts, redaction example and W18 teach-back checklist in accessible form.
Do not invent a correct route or require every real household agreement to be resolved before completion. Institutional/high-rise guidance remains separately review-gated.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 15–18; contact sheet page 17 offline only

missions.title: Say What the Listener Needs
missions.purpose: Rehearse an accurate simulated call and a useful household check-in, then improve both.
missions.knowledge: Identify location, facts, people, needs, hazards and listening, plus check-in time, scope and status.
missions.skill: Speak or write a fictional call and revise ambiguity after feedback.
missions.desire: Replace pressure to sound certain with permission to say unknown.
missions.action: Perform both communication rehearsals and repeat a corrected part.

blocks.heading: Exercise only
body: Do not dial an emergency number. This activity uses only fictional information and has no live-call mode.
The operator role asks clarifying questions; it must not improvise real operational advice. No recording or transcript upload is required.

blocks.heading: Separate call information from coordination
body: For the simulated call, make location understandable, distinguish observed facts from assumptions and state affected people, needs, hazards and unknowns. Listen to the questions.
A household check-in needs a clear time, the people or area it covers, status, needs and next update. These details help prevent a vague message being read too broadly.

blocks.heading: Retain facts and unknowns
body: The source fictional training-house example includes a blocked road. Keep the supplied observation distinct from what has not been established.
Explain what you know in plain language and say unknown where the scenario does not provide an answer.

blocks.heading: Practise caller and listener
body: Use caller, operator and observer roles, or write and read both sides yourself. The listener can ask for clarification of the fictional facts.
Use the observer fields to find one unclear detail, then revise and repeat that part.

blocks.heading: Allow uncertainty and a pause
body: Which detail is difficult to explain? You may pause, write or say you do not know. Accuracy matters more than sounding certain.

blocks.heading: Make a check-in useful
body: Rewrite the source vague message using the private template. Include time, people or scope, status, need and next update.
Keep a statement about one person or time from becoming an unsupported claim about everyone or every time.

blocks.heading: Confirm two rehearsals and a retry
body: Confirm after the fictional call, the household check-in and an improved second attempt are performed. Keep the before/after comparison private.

blocks.heading: Review clarity
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Use the supplied fictional training-house and blocked-road facts; do not insert real personal details.
Perform a simulated call aloud or in writing, using a partner with consent or playing both roles.
Check location, observation versus assumption, affected people, needs, unknowns and listening against the source observer fields.
Rewrite an unclear detail and repeat it. Then perform a household check-in with time, scope, status, need and next update.
Do not dial or send a real communication. Privately compare the first and revised attempts.
aarPrompts: Could the listener locate the incident?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S06: verify current emergency-call guidance while preserving no-live-practice boundaries; M04-S08: approve status labels; M04-S09: privacy review; M04-S13: BM scripts.
Exact P43 training-house facts, P47 vague message and W20 observer rubric need source extraction and approval before objective checks or full role cards are enabled.
No emergency number, availability claim or dispatcher procedure is supplied in this asset. Communication practice does not certify response competence.

missions.title: Change the Decision When Facts Change
missions.purpose: Complete and revise a two-round tabletop decision worksheet as scenario conditions change.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish scenario-specific movement, suitable shelter and assistance options.
missions.skill: Explain action, supporting fact, support need and a review trigger.
missions.desire: Recognise pressure to keep an earlier answer and choose to revise it.
missions.action: Perform two tabletop decision rounds with changed facts and correct an unsafe assumption.

blocks.heading: Name the fact that changed
body: A decision can change when the facts change. Explain which condition supports your choice and what would trigger another review.

blocks.heading: Keep choices within the scenario
body: Movement, shelter and assistance examples are not a universal decision tree. Current hazards and official directions matter.
This is a tabletop exercise. Do not explore routes, enter floodwater, travel to danger or improvise carrying someone.

blocks.heading: Compare the source conditions
body: The source set includes directed evacuation with a safe usable route; a flooded road; and a safe building with hazardous outdoor conditions and no evacuation direction.
A further source case includes an access-support need. Keep each case’s facts and unknowns distinct.

blocks.heading: Connect choice to evidence
body: For each supplied case, state the action, the supporting fact, any support need and the condition for reviewing the decision.
Do not treat a flooded route as safe, generalise one shelter answer to all hazards or assume assistance has been agreed.

blocks.heading: Question the written route
body: What could happen if a route were treated as safe merely because it is written down? Think about how changing conditions should affect the plan.

blocks.heading: Work two rounds
body: Complete round one privately, then use the source’s changed condition for round two. Mark the changed evidence and revise an assumption.
Include support preferences as agreed or unresolved. No movement, lifting or real evacuation drill is required.

blocks.heading: Confirm the revision happened
body: Confirm after two decisions and a revision are performed. Explain the reasoning privately using the source criteria; it is not AI-scored.

blocks.heading: Review the changed condition
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Use two supplied tabletop rounds and the source condition change. Do not invent a new hazard combination.
For round one, privately state action, supporting fact, support need and review trigger.
For round two, mark the changed evidence and revise at least one assumption or decision.
Keep any support agreement explicitly agreed or unresolved. Do not use a written route as proof of current safety.
Keep all practice on paper or in thought; no route exploration, floodwater crossing, carrying or real movement is needed.
aarPrompts: What would trigger the next review?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S05: approve conditional movement and support; M04-S07: Malaysian preparedness SME must approve scenario scope, changed conditions and feedback; M04-S13: BM review.
Exact W24 feedback and W25 round-condition cards are needed before enabling decisions. Any new hazard combination requires separate approval.
Never supply a safe-depth threshold, universal response tree, invented carrying technique or AI score for free reasoning.

missions.title: Help Without Adding Harm
missions.purpose: Produce a handover-ready fictional coordination record and test a specific correction.
missions.knowledge: Distinguish contacted, positively confirmed, assistance needed and unknown, and know role boundaries.
missions.skill: Link duplicate requests, preserve time, source and scope, and assign follow-up.
missions.desire: Recognise that useful help can mean accurate coordination within your role.
missions.action: Complete the source update exercise, perform a handover read-back and repair an ambiguity.

blocks.heading: Make the record usable for the next person
body: Can another coordinator take over without repeating every question? Use a fictional record and preserve what is known and unknown.

blocks.heading: Keep status dimensions distinct
body: Contacted, positively confirmed, assistance needed and unknown describe different aspects of an update. A contact attempt does not prove safety.
Keep source, time, status, need, owner and next update clear. These are training categories, not official response codes or authority.

blocks.heading: Read the fictional update stream
body: The source timeline includes duplicate transport requests in A, four people reported safe in B, no reply in C and an unknown new destination.
Link duplicates without losing the need. Preserve the time and scope of B, keep C unknown and mark the destination instruction unverified.

blocks.heading: Build one fictional record
body: Privately record source, time, status, need, owner and next update. Make uncertainty visible and avoid repeating a request as though it were a new need.
Do not turn the worksheet into a real resident database or include public diagnoses and personal contact lists.

blocks.heading: Recovery questions do not certify safety
body: Receding water is not an all-clear. Official directions and structural, electrical, access or contamination concerns may require competent help.
Do not enter danger to inspect, dispatch volunteers into danger, inspect electrical systems or undertake hazardous cleanup for this exercise.

blocks.heading: Choose useful help within your role
body: Which apparently helpful act could hide a need or exceed your role? Accurate information, a clear handoff and an honest unknown can be useful contributions.

blocks.heading: Read back and repair
body: Read the record as the next coordinator, alone or with a consenting partner. Find a duplicated or unclear field and repair it.
Apply recovery questions to the fictional setting to identify unknowns, not to certify re-entry.

blocks.heading: Confirm the handover and correction
body: Confirm after performing a handover and making a specific revision. Keep the record private.

blocks.heading: Review the improvement
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.

actionInstructions: Complete the supplied fictional update stream in one record with source, time, status, need, owner and next update.
Link duplicate requests without deleting the underlying need. Retain the safe report’s time and scope, no-reply uncertainty and unverified destination.
Perform a partner or solo handover read-back and revise one unclear or duplicated field.
Privately apply the recovery questions to identify unknowns without inspecting a real hazard or certifying safety.
Choose how you would check whether the correction helps the next coordinator.
aarPrompts: How will you check the improvement?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S08: approve coordinator roles/status categories; M04-S09: privacy and minimum-information review; M04-S10: approve recovery and competent-help boundary; M04-S13: BM review.
Supply the full timestamped P60/W28 update stream, approved handover checklist and recovery questions. The synopsis here does not invent missing times or destinations.
No real resident database, public diagnosis list, volunteer dispatch, re-entry certification or electrical inspection instructions may be created from this activity.

missions.title: Prove the Pack Can Be Used
missions.purpose: Use the complete readiness pack in a two-stage source scenario, correct gaps and prepare a realistic next cycle.
missions.knowledge: Retrieve the ten source-tested principles and the programme’s awareness limits.
missions.skill: Connect information, backup communication, inclusive support and changed movement conditions.
missions.desire: Choose a feasible next conversation, preparation and practice without pretending consent exists.
missions.action: Enact the two-stage tabletop scenario, revise the pack and rehearse one next step before completion.

blocks.heading: Use the pack to answer a new household’s needs
body: Use the pack rather than memory alone. Follow the source household through two stages and identify what the changed facts require you to reconsider.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Information, communication and conditions change
body: The source fictional Mei, Raj, Anya and Dev scenario includes failed chat and a preference for written messages.
The second stage changes an instruction, route and helper arrangement. Keep the new facts separate from assumptions carried over from stage one.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Apply the pack across both stages
body: Privately explain how the pack supports information, communication, inclusive support and movement decisions in each stage.
Identify a gap revealed by the changed conditions and revise the relevant part of the pack. Keep all activity tabletop-based.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Trace the connected pack
body: Review the baseline, information map, preparation priorities, plan, communication practice, decision worksheet, coordination record and integrated scenario.
Trace an open agreement from the baseline to the plan and follow-up so it remains visible rather than being silently treated as resolved.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Plan a feasible next cycle
body: Privately choose a conversation, a preparation task and a practice activity, with realistic owners and dates.
Keep an agreement unresolved until the relevant person agrees. A future commitment supports the next cycle but does not replace the activity performed now.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Rehearse one next step now
body: Use the fictional pack to rehearse a chosen conversation or demonstrate a safe preparation step now. A solo rehearsal is valid.
Revise the pack based on what the attempt shows. Real follow-through can happen privately after the course.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Confirm integration, revision and rehearsal
body: Confirm only after both scenario stages, a pack revision and a present-tense rehearsal are performed. Keep all pack contents and correction reasoning private.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Review transfer to changed conditions
body: Think privately or use your own offline notes. Do not submit reflection writing or personal information. Choose one improvement for the next attempt.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

blocks.heading: Understand the completion scope
body: The programme records awareness learning and self-declared practice after its required learning gates are satisfied.
It does not confer rescue qualification, accreditation, clinical competence or emergency-response authority. Keep practising within your limits.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37

actionInstructions: Use the complete fictional readiness pack for both stages of the supplied Mei/Raj/Anya/Dev scenario.
Privately connect information, backup communication, support preferences and current-condition decisions, marking the facts that change.
Revise one revealed gap and trace an unresolved agreement across the baseline, plan and follow-up.
Choose three realistic next actions with owners and dates, then rehearse one conversation or safe preparation step now.
After the approved assessment becomes available, review and retry as required and correct every designated critical error. Keep correction reasoning private.
Choose the pack revision you will test in the next cycle.
aarPrompts: Which revision will you test next?
reviewNotes: DRAFT — human safety, instructional and accessibility review required before learner publication.
M04-S06: emergency-call guidance review; M04-S07: conditional-scenario review; M04-S11: bank/rationales and awareness completion policy; M04-S12: source attribution correction; M04-S13: BM review.
The canonical source bank M04-Q01–Q10 maps to P71–80/W32–33 with feedback P81–82/W34–35. Questions, answer keys and hidden grading logic are omitted from this public asset.

Source policy awaiting approval: at least 8/10, every designated safety-critical error corrected through an approved retry, and all eight activity components completed. No scores, attempts or narratives persist.
Supply the complete two-stage scenario, approved connected-pack checklist and versioned assessment outside the public bundle. Every outstanding campaign review must be resolved before publication.
sourceRefs: M04-W pages 31–39; pack review 36, private next actions 37
